No.796 of 2015 on the files of the Court of the Additional Sessions Judge-I, Thrissur.

sentences.text: 2. The victim in the case was a child aged 3  years.
The victim was residing with her grandparents and mother at the time of occurrence.
The mother of the child was away at her place of employment at the relevant time.
The father of the child was not with the child and her mother on account of matrimonial discord.
The accused is a person who resides in the house adjacent to the house of child.

The case 2024:KER:93224 was registered on a complaint lodged by the mother of the child and the investigation in the case revealed that on 03.10.2015, at about 4.00 p.m., when the child went to the house of the accused to watch television, the accused committed rape and penetrative sexual assault on her.
Final report was accordingly filed against the accused.

3. On the accused being committed to trial, the Special Court framed charges against the accused under Section 376 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and Sections 4 and 6 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (the POCSO Act).

sentences.text: Since the accused pleaded not guilty to the charges, the prosecution examined witnesses on its side and proved through them the documents relied on by it.
When the incriminating evidence was put to the accused thereupon, he denied the same and maintained that he is innocent.
Since the Special Court did not find the case to be one fit for acquittal, the accused was called upon to enter on his defence.
A witness was examined by the accused at that stage.
Thereupon, on a consideration of the matters before it, the Special Court found 2024:KER:93224 the accused not guilty of the charges and acquitted him.
The State is aggrieved by the said decision of the Special Court, hence this appeal.

4. Heard the learned Special Public Prosecutor and the learned counsel for the respondent.
5.
The only evidence in the case is the evidence tendered by the child.
It is seen that the Special Court took the view that it is not safe to convict the accused solely based on the testimony of the child.
The impugned judgment was passed accordingly.

As the appeal is one preferred under Section 378 of the Code of Criminal Procedure against the order of acquittal, the question to be considered State Of Kerala vs Itty on 11 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16372566/

sentences.text: The point that falls for consideration is whether the view taken by the Special Court can be said to be a reasonable one on the facts of the case.
7. In order to adjudicate the point, it is necessary to have an idea about the evidence in the case.
PW1 is the mother of the child.
PW1 had not seen the occurrence.
As stated, she was away on the alleged day in a house where she was working as a domestic help.
According to PW1, the child was being taken care of by her parents.

PW1 deposed that when she asked the child about the occurrence on receiving information from her mother, the child informed PW1 that the accused removed her undergarment and placed his genital organ on her vagina when she went to his house to watch television.

The expression used by the child to convey the sexual assault on her, according to PW1,
was that "           ".
It was deposed by PW1 that the child was examined by the doctor at the Taluk Hospital, Kodungallur on 09.10.2015.

In cross-examination, PW1 stated that the child used to play with the grandchildren of the 2024:KER:93224 accused and that there was a quarrel between her family and the family of the accused about two months prior to the occurrence.
In cross-examination, PW1 has also stated that the accused had misbehaved with her also once before her marriage.

The suggestion made to PW1 by the counsel for the accused in cross-examination was that the allegation was raised on account of a misunderstanding, and of course, the said suggestion was denied by PW1.
8. PW2 is the child herself.
Before recording the evidence of the child, the Special Court conducted voir dire to satisfy itself as regards the competency of the child to testify.
PW2 identified the accused in the dock and deposed that she used to visit his house to watch television and the occurrence took place on one of such occasions.
As regards the occurrence, the evidence tendered by the child was that " .      ".
The said evidence was given by the child after pointing to her private part.
Thereupon, the child repeated "    .  '  (".
It was deposed by PW2 that she informed the occurrence to her grandmother, Parvathy and 2024:KER:93224 her grandmother, in turn, informed the occurrence to the mother of the child.
PW2 affirmed in her evidence that she gave statement to the Magistrate.

In cross-examination,
when PW2 was asked as to whether she knows one Unnimaman, another person residing in the neighbourhood of the house of the child, she answered in the affirmative.
Later, when PW2 was asked as to whether Unnimaman had assaulted her, she replied in the negative.
Further, when PW2 was asked as to whether she informed the Magistrate as to whether Unnimaman had sexually assaulted her, she replied in the negative.
When PW2 was confronted with the question whether she informed the Magistrate that Unnimaman also assaulted her sexually, her answer was that it was simply stated by her (  ).

When PW2 was questioned as to whether she was instructed by anyone to tell the court that the accused sexually assaulted her, her answer was that her mother State Of Kerala vs Itty on 11 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16372566/
3 instructed her to say so.

sentences.text: In cross-examination, it was also affirmed by PW2 that even after the occurrence, she used to go to the house of the accused to watch television.
PW3 is the grandmother of the child.
The version of PW3 was that when she observed that the child was not playful and asked the child as to the reason for the same, the child informed PW3 that the accused assaulted her sexually.
It was also deposed by PW3 that she noticed some discolouration (  ) in her genital area while bathing her.

In the cross-examination, when PW3 was asked as to whether there was a quarrel between her family and the family of the accused, PW3 though initially took the stand that it was a trivial issue and that the same was solved then and there, later she admitted that the quarrel arose on account of the allegation that her husband twisted the hand of the grandson of the accused and that it ultimately resulted in a big quarrel.

It was clarified by PW3 in her evidence that the child did not tell her that the occurrence took place on 03.10.2015 and the said date was an inference made by PW3 based on the information furnished by the child.
PW6 was the doctor who conducted the medical examination of the child at the Taluk Headquarters Hospital, Kodungallur at 6.45 a.m. on 09.10.2015.

It was deposed by PW6 that the history was given to her by the child herself as " <=        ' .

According to PW6, on physical examination, there was no injury on the body of the child and the child was complaining of frequent micturition.
It was also deposed by PW6 that on local examination, no abrasion or injuries was noticed on the vulva, and the hymen was intact.
Ext.P2 is the certificate of medical examination.
During cross-examination, the suggestion made by the counsel for the accused to PW6 was that the history of the case was given to her by the mother of the child, and PW6 denied that suggestion.
PW10 was the police officer who conducted the investigation in the case.
It was deposed by PW10 that the time of the alleged occurrence was not stated in Ext.P1 First Information Statement and the time of the alleged occurrence was subsequently ascertained by him.

According to 2024:KER:93224 PW10, he had no occasion to peruse the statement of the child recorded by the Magistrate as the same was received by him only after submitting the final report, and as such, he had not conducted any investigation about the person named Unnimaman referred to by the child in Ext.P3 statement given to the Magistrate.

As revealed from the evidence discussed above, the only direct substantive evidence to prove the occurrence as alleged by the prosecution is the evidence of the child.

Even though the prosecution relied on the evidence tendered by PW6, the doctor who conducted the medical examination of the child, the evidence tendered by PW6 does not, in any manner, support the case of the prosecution.
True, it was deposed by PW6 that the history of the case was stated to her by the child herself.

sentences.text: Having regard to the nature of the evidence tendered by the child as PW2, the 2024:KER:93224 manner in which PW2 narrated the occurrence in court and also the manner in which PW2 stated to have narrated the occurrence to PW1 and PW3, it is doubtful as to whether PW2 would have made such a statement to the doctor, as the statement appeared to us to be very formal as opposed to how the child stated the occurrence to PWs 1 and 3.
Be that as it may, PW6 has categorically stated in her evidence that she did not find any injuries on the body of the child when the medical examination was conducted.

In fact, in the evidence tendered by PW3, the grandmother of the child, it is stated that she noticed a discolouration in the genital area of the child when she was bathing her, PW6 doctor had not noticed such discolouration.

Had there been such discolouration in the genital area of the child, PW6 would have certainly noticed the same at the time of her examination, especially since the child was taken to the doctor on the very same day.
The conclusion arrived at by PW6 after the medical examination was that there is no evidence of recent or past vaginal penetration.
The evidence tendered by PW1 and PW3 are relied on by the prosecution only to corroborate the version of the child that she disclosed the occurrence to them.
In this context, it is relevant to point out that another witness was also cited by the prosecution to prove that the child narrated the occurrence to the said witness also.
The said witness was a teacher of the child in her nursery school namely, Sheela.
The prosecution, however, chose not to examine her in the case.

Inasmuch as PWs 1 and 3 are the mother and grandmother of the child, according to us, this being a case where the child disclosed about the occurrence to a person other than relatives, Sheela should have also been examined as a witness in the case.

The daughter-in-law of the accused namely, Abida was cited by the prosecution to prove the fact that she found the child running out from the house of the accused frightened, and the accused looked perplexed at the relevant time.
Strangely, the prosecution chose not to examine the said witness as well.
13. There cannot be any doubt that the evidence of a rape victim can be the sole basis of a conviction.
But, it is 2024:KER:93224 trite that in order to base a conviction solely on the evidence of the rape victim, such evidence shall be of a sterling quality.
In Rai Sandeep v. State (NCT of Delhi), (2012) 8 SCC 21, the Apex Court had occasion to consider the question as to who can be said to be a sterling witness.

entities.text: Rai Sandeep v. State (NCT of Delhi), (2012) 8 SCC 21
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Paragraph 22 of the judgment of the Apex Court in the said case reads thus:
"In our considered opinion, the "sterling witness" should be of a very high quality and calibre whose version should, therefore, be unassailable.
The court considering the version of such witness should be in a position to accept it for its face value without any hesitation.
To test the quality of such a witness, the status of the witness would be immaterial and what would be relevant is the truthfulness of the statement made by such a witness.

What would be more relevant would be the consistency of the statement right from the starting point till the end, namely, at the time when the witness makes the initial statement and ultimately before the court.

It should be State Of Kerala vs Itty on 11 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16372566/
5 natural and consistent with the case of the prosecution qua the accused.

entities.text:
State Of Kerala vs Itty on 11 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16372566/
5
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: There should not be any prevarication in the version of such a witness.

The witness should be in a position to withstand the cross- examination of any length and howsoever strenuous it may be and under no circumstance should give room for any doubt as to the factum of the occurrence, the persons involved, as well as the sequence of it.

Such a version should have co-relation with each and every one of other supporting material such as the recoveries made, the weapons used, the manner of offence committed, the scientific evidence and the expert opinion.
The 2024:KER:93224 said version should consistently match with the version of every other witness.

It can even be stated that it should be akin to the test applied in the case of circumstantial evidence where there should not be any missing link in the chain of circumstances to hold the accused guilty of the offence alleged against him.

Only if the version of such a witness qualifies the above test as well as all other such similar tests to be applied, can it be held that such a witness can be called as a "sterling witness" whose version can be accepted by the court without any corroboration and based on which the guilty can be punished.

To be more precise, the version of the said witness on the core spectrum of the crime should remain intact while all other attendant materials, namely, oral,
documentary and material objects should match the said version in material particulars in order to enable the court trying the offence to rely on the core version to sieve the other supporting materials for holding the offender guilty of the charge alleged."

As evident from the decision aforesaid, the evidence of a sterling witness should be one that appears natural and consistent with the case of the prosecution qua the accused and such witnesses under no circumstances, shall give room for any doubt as to the factum of the occurrence.
The moot question therefore, is whether the child in the case on hand can be said to be a sterling witness so as to justify the conviction of the accused solely based on her evidence.
As noticed, the victim in the case is a child who was aged only 3 years at the time of the alleged occurrence.

Even though there is no rule or practice that in every case the evidence of a child witness must be corroborated before a conviction can be allowed to stand, as a rule of prudence, the courts always find it desirable to have corroboration to such evidence from other dependable evidence on record, especially when the evidence is let in by children of tender age.
As noticed, the stand taken by the child when her statement was recorded under Section 164 of the Code was that she was sexually assaulted by another neighbour Unnimaman.

The statement of the child recorded under Section 164 of the Code indicates that it was when the learned Magistrate sought a clarification from the child as to whether anybody else had assaulted her sexually, the child then mentioned the name of the accused.

When she was asked about the correctness of mentioning the name of Unnimaman,
she made a casual statement that she simply stated the same.
This stand of the child creates a serious doubt as to the 2024:KER:93224 reliability of the evidence given by her.
It was all the more so since the child clarified in her evidence that her mother instructed her to give evidence in that fashion.

The relevant portion of the evidence reads thus:

6 "           '  (Q)   (A )"
In the above circumstances, according to us, the Special Court cannot be found at fault with for having taken the stand that the possibility of tutoring the child to give evidence cannot be completely ruled out and therefore, the evidence of the child does not inspire confidence of the court.

sentences.text: The said view, according to us, on the facts and circumstances of the case, can only be said to be a reasonable one.
We take this view also for the reason that the Special Court had the occasion to assess the demeanor of the child.

We take this view also for the reason that admittedly, when the occurrence was alleged to have taken place, the families were not in a cordial relationship as there was a serious quarrel between them on account of the allegation that the grandfather of the child twisted the hand of 2024:KER:93224 one of the grandsons of the accused.
Yet another reason for us to doubt the veracity of the evidence tendered by the victim is the evidence given by PW1 that the accused misbehaved with PW1 also prior to her marriage.
The above circumstances do not also rule out the possibility of a complaint by PW1 on account of the various reasons already discussed above.
In the circumstances, we do not find any reason to interfere with the impugned decision, and the appeal is therefore, dismissed.
